transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-21 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood Marketing), Devon (Redwood SE), Sofia (Everledger Head of Product Marketing), Liam (Everledger CTO)
Recording: yes (podcast-style, permission requested)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks so much for joining. This is Maya from Redwood, I'm the marketing lead. Today we're recording a relaxed customer interview for Redwood's podcast series. We'll keep it conversational — little bit about your story, then some product/tech points, then wrap with a couple of quotes for marketing. Is everyone good with audio recording?

[00:10] Sofia: Yeah, totally fine. We already filled the form but happy to confirm on this call.

[00:15] Liam: Fine by me, thanks.

[00:20] Maya: Great. Okay, quick intro? Sofia — do you want to start with Everledger's elevator? And maybe mention the product where Redwood's inference sits in your stack.

[00:28] Sofia: Sure. So Everledger, we do digital provenance for legal docs, contracts and supply chain records, uh, with a focus on regulated customers. We have a product that ingests contracts and produces summaries, risk flags and clausal mapping — it's used by our legal ops and partner teams. We were looking to make that faster and cheaper to scale.

[00:44] Maya: And Liam, your role?

[00:47] Liam: I'm the CTO, I run the infra and platform teams. We partner with multiple vendors and run two main types of workloads: high-throughput batch for nightly ingest, and low-latency interactive summarization for customers in the UI.

[00:58] Maya: Nice. Can you describe the decision to go with Redwood? What were the main criteria?

[01:06] Sofia: Two big things: predictable costs and data controls. We had a few vendors where projected token costs spiked for long docs, and that made procurement nervous. Second, for some of our enterprise accounts we required private networking and audit logs. Redwood's Dedicated offering addressed both.

[01:22] Devon: If I can jump in — you also had an interesting pattern of mixed workloads, right? Batch jobs with 100k pages overnight and then sub-second responses in the UI. How did the Dedicated pool help with that?

[01:34] Liam: Yeah, the dedicated GPU pools let us partition capacity. We run our batch jobs on a reserved node pool and the interactive route on a low-latency tier. The autoscaling and burst capacity meant we didn't overprovision. Also Redwood's prefix caching — we call it "K V cash" in our notes sometimes — really dropped token usage for repeated templates.

[01:52] Sofia: I will say the quant — the quantization recommendations were helpful too. We saw cost reductions with minimal quality loss.

[02:00] Maya: There's a great soundbite opportunity there — Sofia, could you quantify the cost savings in a sentence?

[02:05] Sofia: Sure. We reduced per-document inference costs by ~45% after switching to Dedicated plus Redwood's batching and quant guidance, while keeping median latency under 400ms for interactive sessions.

[02:18] Maya: Love that. For the audience who might not know, can you explain briefly how you verified the quality didn't degrade?

[02:26] Liam: We ran an A/B against our eval set — a set of 2,000 representative contracts — and measured Rouge-lite scores and human review on a sampled subset. There was a tiny delta in some edge-case legalese, but we tuned prompts and reranking to correct for that.

[02:44] Devon: We had an SE session with Liam's team where we walked through KV cache behavior and the rollout policy — sorry sometimes our docs say K V cache with spaces, it's a speech-to-text artifact — but the important bit is the cache preserved tokenization across sessions which saved a lot.

[02:58] Sofia: Yeah, just to be clear, the thing that saved us was the automatic prefix caching and also the smart batching during nightly runs. There were a few false starts with initial batching settings but Redwood's team recommended adjustments that worked.

[03:14] Maya: Switching to security — many enterprise customers care about SOC 2 and KMS. Can you describe any red flags Everledger raised and how Redwood addressed them?

[03:23] Liam: We required customer-managed keys and VPC peering for our Dedicated deployment. Redwood provided a private deployment variant and direct connect options; their audit logs and trace hooks satisfied our security team. There was a brief question on retention — we asked for guaranteed no persistent storage of raw docs in the hosted path — Redwood's legal clarified retention policies which was fine for us.

[03:46] Maya: The legal and security teams reading this will appreciate that. Quick note for the editor: flag the bit about "no persistent storage" and retention wording.

[03:53] Sofia: Also, the SSO integration and RBAC were straightforward, which made adoption across our product org easier.

[04:00] Maya: Perfect. Now, for the podcast flow, we'd like to include a short technical segment where Devon can explain the engineering tradeoff — maybe 60 seconds — is that okay?

[04:08] Devon: Yeah happy to.

[04:10] Devon: (technical segment) So at a high level, Redwood's runtime optimizes kernel selection and batching; for Everledger we focused on two knobs: batch sizing and quant profiles. Larger batches for batch processing improved throughput and unit cost, but we kept a separate low-latency path with smaller batches for UI traffic. We also used continuous KV caching to avoid repeating prefix tokens which is common in contract templates. The net effect was better utilization on GPUs and more predictable token spend.

[04:49] Liam: That matches our ops view — we also liked the rollout capabilities. Canary deploys let us test new model variants on a subset of traffic and auto-fallback prevented any outages during a bad model push.

[05:03] Maya: Nice. Back to story — can you describe a customer win or example where this mattered?

[05:09] Sofia: One of our large banking customers needed contract redlines in under a second during negotiation. Before Redwood we had a slow path, now negotiating lawyers get summaries and suggested redlines in the UI, which sped up deal cycles. They also liked the audit trail which mapped changes to clauses.

[05:26] Maya: Great anecdote. We'll want a one-sentence quote for the blog post — do you have something now or do you want to provide later?

[05:33] Sofia: I can give a quick one now: "Redwood helped us deliver legal summaries at scale with the cost predictability our enterprise customers require." Might tweak it after hearing the full edit.

[05:43] Maya: That's perfect. We'll capture that.

[05:46] Sofia: Also, small nit — please don't use the internal model name in public, we prefer to keep references to 'Redwood's Dedicated service' rather than exact variant names.

[05:55] Maya: Noted. We'll sanitize internal model references.

[06:00] Liam: On logistics, when will you publish and do we need sign-off from our PR?

[06:06] Maya: Our plan is to publish a short-form blog and a podcast episode two weeks from now. We'll send a transcript and the raw audio for approval. We typically ask for legal/PR sign-off on quotes and logo usage.

[06:18] Sofia: Sounds good. We'll get PR in the loop.

[06:21] Maya: Any concerns about competitive mentions? We might reference the landscape briefly.

[06:26] Liam: No problem, just factual. We mentioned some other vendors internally but nothing sensitive.

[06:30] Devon: Quick technical mis-transcribe note — sometimes Fireflies picks up 'KV' as 'K V' or 'K V cash' — we'll check the transcript.

[06:38] Maya: Thank you. Okay, last part — consents. By default we use the quotes and audio if you approve. We'll send a one-page consent form. Anything else you'd need?

[06:50] Sofia: Please include the option to opt-out of promotional emails.

[06:54] Maya: Will do.

[06:56] Liam: One more technical ask — can Redwood share a simple diagram of the dedicated topology we ran? That helps our engineers cite the architecture in a case study.

[07:05] Devon: Absolutely, I'll share a lightweight diagram and a 2-paragraph blurb on caching and batching.

[07:11] Maya: Excellent. I'll summarize next steps at the end of the raw recording. Thanks again, this was great.

[07:17] Sofia: Thanks, everyone.

[07:20] Liam: Thanks.

[07:22] Maya: Closing notes: Redwood will send audio + draft transcript; Everledger to return quotes and logo approval; SE to provide technical blurb and diagram. We'll aim to publish by 2025-11-04.

[07:36] (end recording)

Notes: transcription contains minor mis-hearings around 'KV cache' and 'quantization' sometimes seen as 'quant' or 'count' — editor should confirm technical terms. References to onboarding docs and diagram will be provided in follow-ups.
